reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / Gorlin's Syndromes of the Head and Neck
clinicalPearls: A relatively common distal arthrogryposis that overlaps with, but is milder than, Freeman-Sheldon syndrome
Hand and foot contractures resemble those of other distal arthrogryposes, with camptodactyly, ulnar deviation and talipes equinovarus
Facial features are subtle: a triangular face, downslanting palpebral fissures, a small mouth and prominent nasolabial folds, but without the severe microstomia or deep chin dimple of Freeman-Sheldon
Caused by variants in the fast-twitch sarcomeric genes TNNI2, TNNT3, TPM2 or MYH3, mostly autosomal dominant
Intellect is normal and there is no progressive weakness
Distinguishing it from Freeman-Sheldon guides prognosis, surgical planning and counselling
Management follows the distal arthrogryposis principles of physiotherapy, splinting, serial casting and selective surgical release
reference.pathophysiology: Sheldon-Hall syndrome results from dominant variants in genes of the fast skeletal muscle contractile complex, chiefly troponin I (TNNI2), troponin T (TNNT3), tropomyosin (TPM2) and occasionally myosin (MYH3). These variants alter the calcium-regulated interaction of actin and myosin and disturb foetal muscle tone. The reduced and unbalanced movement of the developing foetus allows periarticular fibrosis and joint fixation, producing predominantly distal contractures. Because the underlying genes overlap with those of Freeman-Sheldon syndrome, the two conditions form a phenotypic spectrum, with Sheldon-Hall representing the milder end.
additionalDifferentials: Escobar syndrome when webbing is present
additionalInvestigations: Dysmorphology examination comparing facial features with Freeman-Sheldon syndrome
Molecular genetic testing (TNNI2, TNNT3, TPM2, MYH3 panel)
Radiographs of hands, feet and spine
Prenatal ultrasound in at-risk pregnancies for foetal akinesia and fixed posture
Feeding and airway assessment when a small mouth or micrognathia is present
redFlags: Feeding difficulty or airway concern from micrognathia
Progressive scoliosis during growth requiring orthopaedic surveillance
Features suggesting the more severe Freeman-Sheldon end of the spectrum
Signs of progressive weakness pointing to an alternative myopathy
reference.prognosis: The outlook is good, with normal cognition and lifespan; contractures are static and functional outcomes after physiotherapy and orthopaedic surgery are generally favourable, though some residual limb deformity may remain.
pitfalls: Over-diagnosing Freeman-Sheldon syndrome and overstating severity and anaesthetic risk
Missing a mildly affected parent and giving incorrect recurrence risk
Delaying stretching and splinting so that contractures fixate
Overlooking associated scoliosis during childhood follow-up
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
Gorlin's Syndromes of the Head and Neck
management: No disease-specific drug therapy; management centres on physiotherapy with stretching, serial casting, and splinting of distal contractures from early life
Orthopaedic surgery for fixed foot deformity (talipes equinovarus) and residual hand contractures where function is limited
Occupational therapy and orthoses to optimise hand function and independence
Feeding and airway assessment and support when a small mouth or micrognathia is present
Monitor growth, spine for scoliosis, and functional development
Genetic counselling and testing (TNNI2, TNNT3, TPM2, MYH3) with family evaluation given autosomal dominant inheritance
Prenatal counselling and ultrasound surveillance in at-risk pregnancies
Coordinate care through clinical genetics and orthopaedic multidisciplinary teams
